Split the conjunction and treat its two parts independently.

For the asymptotic term, use the Chebyshev bound \(\theta(t)=O(t)\). On \(t\ge 2\), this makes
\[
\frac{\theta(t)}{t(\log t)^2}=O\!\left(\frac1{(\log t)^2}\right).
\]
Split the integral at \(\sqrt x\). The interval \([2,\sqrt x]\) contributes \(O(\sqrt x)\), while on \([\sqrt x,x]\), \(\log t\ge \frac12\log x\), giving \(O(x/\log^2x)\). Both are \(o(x/\log x)\).

For the polynomial identity, work before evaluation. Put \(y=U_n\) and start from its differential equation
\[
(1-X^2)y''=3Xy'-\big((n+1)^2-1\big)y.
\]
Induct on \(k\): differentiate the \(k\)-th identity using the formal product rule. The derivative of \(1-X^2\) changes \(2k+3\) to \(2k+5\), while
\[
(k+1)^2+(2k+3)=(k+2)^2,
\]
producing exactly the next coefficient \((n+1)^2-(k+2)^2\). Finally apply polynomial evaluation at \(x\). This polynomial-level argument uses no division, so it works uniformly over every commutative ring.
